interviewQuestions.question: How would you reconstruct a binary tree given its preorder and inorder traversals, and what makes your solution O(n) instead of O(n²)?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I use two facts about the traversals: preorder's first remaining element is always the current subtree's root, and once I know the root's value, its position in the inorder sequence splits everything into the left subtree (elements before it) and right subtree (elements after it) — because that's literally what inorder means, left subtree then node then right subtree.

The algorithm recurses on that split: take the next unused preorder value as the root, find it in inorder to get the split point, recurse on the left inorder range using the preorder elements that immediately follow, then recurse on the right range using whatever preorder elements remain.

The naive version of 'find the root's value in inorder' is a linear scan, which done once per recursive call makes the whole algorithm O(n²) in the worst case. I avoid that by precomputing a value-to-index map for the inorder array upfront, in one O(n) pass — every subsequent lookup becomes O(1), and since there are exactly n recursive calls doing O(1) work each (beyond the map), the whole reconstruction is O(n).

One assumption I'd confirm upfront: this only works correctly if all values are unique. With duplicates, the value-to-index map collapses distinct positions together, and the reconstruction can become genuinely ambiguous, not just harder to implement.

**Testing:** whether you can both derive the recursive structure and identify the specific optimization that changes the complexity class.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Construction

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't you reconstruct a binary tree uniquely from just its preorder and postorder traversals?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The ambiguity is specifically about nodes with exactly one child. Both preorder and postorder tell you the node comes before or after its subtrees as a whole, but neither tells you *which side* a lone child sits on — inorder is the only one of the three that places the node between its two children, which is precisely what reveals that information.

Concrete example: a root valued 1 with a single child valued 2. If 2 is the left child, preorder is [1, 2] and postorder is [2, 1]. If 2 is instead the right child, preorder is still [1, 2] and postorder is still [2, 1] — identical sequences, two genuinely different trees. No amount of clever indexing recovers the missing information, because the information was never encoded in these two sequences to begin with.

The one case where preorder+postorder does work is a **full** binary tree — every node has either zero or two children, never exactly one — because the single-child ambiguity simply can't occur there. That's a real, sometimes-tested special case, but it's worth stating explicitly as an assumption rather than assuming it silently, since the general claim (any two of the three traversals suffice) is false.

I'd flag this distinction directly if asked to implement preorder+postorder reconstruction, since silently assuming it always works is a common, wrong assumption.

**Testing:** whether you understand traversal information content precisely enough to know when a construction is fundamentally impossible, not just hard.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Ambiguity

interviewQuestions.question: How would you design a serialize/deserialize scheme for a binary tree so the exact original structure is always recoverable?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The key requirement is encoding **null positions explicitly**, since that's exactly the information a single traversal alone doesn't carry (and as we've established, even a pair of traversals without inorder can't reliably carry it either). Once null markers are explicit, a single traversal becomes fully self-describing.

My default: preorder with a sentinel for missing children. Serialize recursively — write the current node's value, then recursively serialize left, then right; when a child is missing, write a sentinel token like `"#"` instead of recursing. Deserialize by reading tokens in the same order: pull the next token, and if it's the sentinel, that subtree is null; otherwise create a node and recursively fill its left and right from the remaining tokens. Both directions are O(n), single pass, no auxiliary index-map needed the way construction-from-a-pair does.

I'd also mention the alternative — level-order with nulls, matching how trees are often visualized as `[1,2,3,null,null,4,5]` — as a valid choice when matching an existing external format matters more than compactness; it needs a queue and careful tracking of when a level is fully null to stop, and it can produce a noticeably larger output on skewed trees, since every missing child at every level needs its own marker.

I'd lead with preorder+nulls unless the interviewer specifically wants the array-style format, since it's simpler to implement correctly and more compact in the typical case.

**Testing:** whether you understand serialization as 'add exactly the missing information' rather than reaching for a specific format by memorized habit.
